The decisive test is whether a government defeat is still possible and would be accepted.

questions.q: 'The choice of electoral system matters less than its advocates claim.' Assess with reference to at least two countries that have changed their electoral system.
markScheme: Sets out what reformers claim: proportionality, the party system, representation, accountability, governance
Mechanical v psychological effects; district magnitude as the key variable
New Zealand 1996 FPTP to MMP: multipartism, coalition government, more Māori and women MPs
Italy (1993, 2005, 2017 reforms) or Japan (1994 move to a parallel system): limited or unexpected effects
Germany 2023 reform or the UK devolved systems (AMS, STV) as evidence
Countervailing forces: social cleavages, party strategy, regional concentration (Cox; Duverger at district level)
Endogeneity: systems are chosen by parties expecting benefits (Boix; Colomer)
Effects take time as voters and parties learn
Unintended consequences (e.g. Scottish 2011 SNP majority under AMS)
Balanced conclusion: strong mechanical effects on proportionality, weaker and context-dependent effects on behaviour and governance
questions.modelAnswer:
Advocates of electoral reform claim that systems shape proportionality, the number of parties, who gets elected, accountability and the quality of government. The evidence supports strong effects on some of these and weak ones on others.

Mechanical effects on proportionality are reliable. New Zealand's switch from FPTP to MMP in 1996 sharply reduced disproportionality. The effective number of parliamentary parties rose, no party won an outright majority until Labour in 2020, and the representation of women and Māori increased. This is strong evidence that rules matter, as Lijphart and Taagepera and Shugart predict.

Other reforms show weaker or unexpected effects. Japan's 1994 move from the single non-transferable vote to a parallel mixed system aimed to end factional, candidate-centred politics and bring two-party alternation. Alternation happened in 2009, but the LDP's dominance soon returned. Italy's repeated reforms (1993, 2005, 2017) were meant to bring stable bipolar competition, yet fragmentation and unstable coalitions persisted, because the parties and cleavages reshaped how the rules worked.

The UK's devolved systems show further limits. AMS in Scotland was expected to prevent single-party majorities, but the SNP won an outright majority in 2011. The highly proportional STV system in Northern Ireland coexists with a party system rooted in the national-identity cleavage, which the electoral system did not create.

There are several reasons the effects are limited. Duverger's law operates at district level, so regional concentration can sustain many parties under FPTP. Social cleavages and party strategy also mediate how rules work. Parties choose systems they expect to benefit from (Boix, 1999), so reforms often confirm existing trends rather than cause them. Effects also take time to appear as voters learn to vote strategically.

The proposition is therefore half right. Electoral systems reliably shape proportionality and representation, but their effects on party systems and the quality of government depend on cleavages, geography and elite strategy, so reformers' bolder claims are usually overstated.

questions.q: Explain the evolution of party organisation from the mass party to the cartel party, and evaluate whether the cartel thesis fits contemporary Britain.
markScheme: Mass party (Duverger): membership-based, rooted in social milieux, financed by dues
Catch-all party (Kirchheimer): broader appeal, weaker ideology, stronger leaders
Electoral-professional party (Panebianco): professional staff and media
Cartel party (Katz and Mair 1995): reliance on the state, collusion, distance from civil society
UK evidence for: Short money and Policy Development Grants, professionalisation, declining membership in the long term
UK evidence against: limited state funding; competition intense; new entrants (Reform UK, Greens) win seats
Membership surges (e.g. Labour after 2015) complicate the picture
Reasoned judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
Duverger's mass party was built on paying members, branches and close links to social groups such as trade unions or churches, which funded it and supplied its activists. Kirchheimer (1966) identified a shift towards catch-all parties that played down ideology to win voters across classes and gave more power to leaders. Panebianco (1988) described electoral-professional parties run by media and polling professionals rather than activists. Katz and Mair (1995) argued that parties then became a cartel: as members and social roots weakened, parties turned to the state for resources and colluded to protect themselves from challengers, becoming agents of the state.

Some British evidence fits. Opposition parties receive state funding through Short money, and parties can claim Policy Development Grants. Campaigning is highly professional and centrally controlled. Membership has fallen dramatically since the 1950s.

But Britain is a weak fit overall. State funding is small by European standards, and the main parties depend heavily on donors and, for Labour, trade unions. Competition is intense rather than collusive: FPTP punishes losers severely, and challengers have broken through. Reform UK won five seats and about 14% of the vote in 2024 and led national opinion polls through much of 2025, while the Greens won four seats. Membership surges, such as Labour's rise to over half a million under Corbyn, show that parties can still mobilise from below.

The cartel thesis captures the professionalisation and statist drift of British parties, but the absence of substantial state funding and the persistent electoral openness mean Britain is closer to the electoral-professional model.

questions.q: Dr Okafor wants to explain why some European democracies introduced generous paid parental leave in the 2000s while others did not. She has funding to study either four countries in depth or 30 OECD democracies statistically. Her preliminary reading suggests that partisanship, women's representation and EU membership may all matter. Advise her on research design, case selection and the main threats to valid inference.
markScheme: Identifies the outcome and plausible explanatory variables (e.g. party in government, female representation, welfare regime, labour-market institutions)
Explains the large-N option: tests general relationships and controls for confounders, but has limited depth and faces measurement problems
Explains the small-N option: process tracing reveals mechanisms and sequencing
Proposes a coherent case-selection strategy (e.g. MSSD using similar welfare regimes with different outcomes, or a typical/deviant case logic)
Warns against selecting on the dependent variable
Notes Galton's problem: diffusion through EU directives and policy learning
Addresses conceptual equivalence: defining 'generous' leave consistently (paid weeks, replacement rate, father quotas)
Recommends a justified design, possibly nested mixed methods (Lieberman 2005)
questions.modelAnswer:
Dr Okafor should first define the outcome precisely. 'Generous' leave could mean paid weeks, the earnings replacement rate or reserved fathers' quotas, and using one consistent measure prevents conceptual stretching. Plausible explanations include left or Green parties in government, women's share of legislative seats, welfare-regime type and labour shortages.

A 30-country statistical design would show whether these factors are associated with generous leave across the OECD while controlling for others. Its limits are the small number of cases for regression, possible differences in how leave schemes are measured, and its inability to show how decisions were made.

A four-country design allows process tracing of how reforms passed: who proposed them, which coalitions supported them and whether EU directives or neighbouring models mattered. A most similar systems design could pair similar countries with different outcomes, for example two conservative-corporatist welfare states where one expanded paid leave substantially and the other did not. She must avoid choosing only generous cases, since that would be selecting on the dependent variable.

Galton's problem is serious here. EU directives on parental leave and cross-national policy learning mean the cases are not independent, so she should code diffusion explicitly.

The strongest option is a nested design (Lieberman, 2005). A quick large-N analysis using existing OECD family database indicators would identify patterns and pick out typical and deviant cases. In-depth case studies would then trace mechanisms. This combines breadth with causal depth and makes her conclusions more credible.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by 'cohabitation' in the French Fifth Republic and why it shifts power within the executive.
markScheme: Defines cohabitation: a president and a prime minister (with an assembly majority) from opposing camps
Explains that the PM depends on the National Assembly, so the president must appoint someone acceptable to the majority
Power shifts to the PM over domestic policy, while the president retains a strong role in foreign affairs and defence; gives an example (1986–88, 1993–95 or 1997–2002)
questions.modelAnswer: Cohabitation occurs when the French president faces a National Assembly majority from the opposing camp and must appoint a prime minister from that majority, because the government is accountable to the Assembly. Real control of domestic policy then passes to the prime minister and government, while the president keeps influence over foreign policy and defence, the so-called reserved domain. Examples include Mitterrand with Chirac (1986–88) and Chirac with Jospin (1997–2002). Aligning the presidential and legislative terms from 2002 made cohabitation less likely.
